raw_response:
*Reasoning in my own voice:*

Ai, you want to know how I farm? Let me think. I've been on this land since I married in, 36 years now. My man and me, we're both getting on. The children are gone to the city for work, so it's just us two at home. We used to do more cotton when we were younger, but picking cotton bends your back and my knees aren't what they were. So now most of the land is wheat and maize, and only a small piece still cotton.

I have 15 mu. About 4 mu I keep in cotton — that's the piece down by the road, the soil there is a bit sandier and cotton does alright on it. The other 11 mu is the good flat ground, and I do wheat in winter and maize in summer on the same land, like everyone around here. That way the land is never empty.

The wheat is already up — I put it in last October, same week as my neighbor old Zhang. This spring I'll give it water when it starts to green up, then again around when it's jointing, and one more before it heads out. Three waterings, same as always. If the sky is dry maybe one more, but the well costs money to run, so we watch it. For topdressing I'll put down about half a bag of urea per mu when I do the green-up water — that's what's worked for me. Before planting I already put a bag of the 15-15-15 compound per mu, that's the base. In June we cut the wheat with the combine — my nephew drives one and charges us a little less than the outside drivers, so we use him.

Right after the wheat comes off, we have to get the maize in fast, maybe three or four days. No time to plow proper — we just drill the maize straight into the stubble. The seed store sells us the Zhengdan variety or whatever is fresh that year, my man goes and picks. For the maize I do like the wheat, a bag of compound at planting, then one full bag of urea when it's knee-high. Maize doesn't need as much water here if the rains come, but if July is dry I'll water it once, maybe twice.

The cotton I start in late April when the soil is warm. Cotton is the most trouble — you're out there all summer spraying for bugs, pulling weeds, and then picking and picking from September into October. That's why I keep the piece small. I use less fertilizer on cotton than on the grain — too much and you get all leaves and no bolls, my father-in-law taught me that long ago.

Money-wise, we're careful. Last year fertilizer went up again and I was worried, but the wheat price was also up a little so it came out okay. I don't borrow for inputs. Whatever cash we have from last harvest is what I spend. If it's not enough, I cut back on the extra urea before I cut back on water.

That's how it goes. Same as last year, more or less, unless something strange happens.
